gendered_legal_restrictions.assessment: Extensive documented menarcheal-seclusion cosmology: a secluded girl is symbolically equated with the potency of the new moon and !Khwa (the Rain); violating seclusion rules is narrated as having severe consequences (a man who looks at her turns to stone/tree). No equivalent seclusion/restriction practice documented for post-pubescent men — an asymmetric, sex-specific regulatory system as recorded.

sources.citation: Hewitt, Roger. Structure, Meaning and Ritual in the Narratives of the Southern San. 1986.
sources.author: Roger Hewitt

ideological_patriarchy.assessment: DISPUTED/genuinely mixed evidence. Female figures are cosmologically significant and not uniformly subordinate (the "Girl who made the Milky Way" narrative centers a female creator-figure), but the menarcheal-girl material frames female reproductive potency as simultaneously powerful and dangerous to men — a "potency-as-danger" framing distinct from a simple subordination/celebration binary. Anne Solomon, "Mythic Women": A Study in Variability in San Rock Art and Narrative (in Lewis-Williams & Dowson, eds., Contested Images, Witwatersrand UP, 1994), concludes gender representation in San rock art/narrative does not reduce to one settled pattern and varies across sites/groups/genres — that non-conclusion is itself the most defensible finding.

sources.citation: Solomon, Anne. "'Mythic Women': A Study in Variability in San Rock Art and Narrative." In Contested Images: Diversity in Southern African Rock Art Research, eds. Lewis-Williams and Dowson. Witwatersrand University Press, 1994.
sources.author: Anne Solomon

dimensions.notes: /Xam is a distinct group/period from Ju/'hoansi (gs_juhoansi) — do not merge these two GenderSystem records into one "San" verdict. Evidentiary base is almost entirely the 1870s-1880s Bleek-Lloyd archive, filtered through Victorian transcription and a coercive collection context (informants were Cape Colony prisoners).
